Regulatory Transformation

Regulatory Transformation: navigating emerging risks, driving AI adoption and reducing regulatory burden

Regulators are facing a shifting operating environment as technology, markets, environmental pressures and societal expectations evolve faster than traditional regulatory frameworks. Fragmented data and limited intelligence continue to make risk prioritisation difficult.

There is a growing opportunity to use advanced analytics to better target regulatory effort. Many regulators are still working to integrate data across systems, uplift analytical capability and embed insights into everyday decision-making.

AI adoption is also becoming a core regulatory transformation issue. Regulators are seeking to balance opportunities for automation and improved risk identification with the need to manage governance, transparency, bias, legal risk, privacy and public confidence.

At the same time, governments are under pressure to reduce red tape, make faster decisions and manage fiscal constraints. This is driving interest in regulatory consolidation, shared-service models and more consistent approaches to regulatory delivery, while maintaining fairness and strong outcomes.

Regulation Hub Intelligence Brief

AI Brief 132 articles across 8 categories

Three regulator investment cycles are converging this fortnight and each carries a discrete advisory window: ASIC's declared strategic reset to 'easier to deal with, harder to avoid' under its incoming chair is simultaneously a client-recalibration event and a transformation advisory mandate for the regulator itself; the AER's published Strategic Plan signals sustained capability and technology uplift across the National Electricity and Gas Markets, creating a pre-tender runway for KPMG's energy-transition and regulatory-strategy practice; and AMSA's Annual Regulatory Program 2026-27 locks in enforcement campaigns across fatigue, cargo securing, and seafarer medical fitness that will generate compliance program demand from maritime operators before the inspection cycle opens. EPBC reform has moved from legislation to implementation with new National Environmental Standards now in force, compressing the compliance runway for mining, infrastructure, and major-property proponents — Q4 2026 is the live conversion window before project pipelines absorb the new approval framework under competitive pressure. Leadership transitions at Victoria's Department of Transport and Planning and the ATSB are classic first-100-days BD events: both appointments create demand for capability reviews and strategic reset advisory that KPMG can pursue without a formal competitive process if it moves in the next four weeks. The NHVR's public declaration of enforcement focus on deliberate avoidance behaviour and the concurrent commencement of HVNL reforms together mark the beginning of an active penalty cycle for heavy vehicle operators — freight clients without current compliance program maturity are immediately exposed. The overarching BD signal across the fortnight is enforcement cycle initiation: ASIC, NHVR, EPA Victoria, and AUSTRAC are all in declared or active enforcement uplift, and the advisory window is shortest for clients who have not yet commissioned independent assurance or compliance gap reviews.

Cross-category themes

Across all sectors, regulators are simultaneously intensifying enforcement posture and advancing dense legislative reform agendas, creating a compounding compliance burden where clients must respond to active scrutiny while redesigning frameworks for imminent structural change. Data governance obligations are the sharpest cross-cutting pressure, with Privacy Act erasure rights, ATO-AUSTRAC data sharing, cross-agency integration reform, and Defence data access frameworks collectively signalling that data compliance is no longer sector-specific but a firm-wide advisory priority.

Tech & AI

National Cabinet convened this fortnight specifically on AI datacentre development, with NSW simultaneously progressing data centre policy reform — infrastructure investment is now a cabinet-level priority, not a departmental pilot, and the advisory window for location strategy, planning approvals, and digital infrastructure frameworks is open now. The Department of Finance is actively working to overcome barriers to cross-agency data sharing and integration, signalling imminent demand for data architecture, interoperability frameworks, and governance uplift across Commonwealth portfolios. EPA Victoria has contracted SenSen Networks for acoustic camera deployment, confirming that state environmental regulators are procuring AI-enabled enforcement tools in production — a procurement pattern that will replicate across other state EPAs and infrastructure regulators within 12 months. The Ashurst/Perkins Coie automated decision-making series' explicit shift to 'defensible decision-making' mirrors what Commonwealth and state oversight bodies are now demanding from agencies, moving ADM governance from a legal-team conversation to a board-level accountability requirement. ACNC is extending cyber security support to charities and NFPs, indicating that regulators with community-sector oversight mandates are expanding their digital risk remit beyond their own operations and into the entities they regulate. The most commercially active clients in this cycle are Department of Finance, EPA Victoria, ACNC, and NSW Government — each at a different AI and data maturity point but all generating concrete advisory demand within the next 90 days.

Capability reviews

Four regulators published or advanced corporate plans this fortnight, signalling a synchronised round of internal capability investment that creates a concentrated BD window before the 2026-27 budget cycle closes. APSC's 2026-27 Corporate Plan resets the APS-wide capability agenda at a moment when agencies are absorbing machinery-of-government changes and tightening workforce data obligations — APSC is both a client and a force-multiplier whose plan shapes every other agency's capability spend. ACMA's 2026-27 plan signals an operating model refresh as spectrum management and online-safety enforcement mandates expand simultaneously, stretching internal capability well beyond current establishment. TEQSA's 2026-30 Corporate Plan is the longest horizon signal: a four-year strategic reset requiring measurable uplift in provider-risk assessment, quality assurance, and digital regulatory capability — a mandate that cannot be met from existing headcount alone. AUSTRAC's Pacific capability program is the most operationally live: real funding is flowing into AML/CTF regulatory capacity-building across Pacific jurisdictions, with AUSTRAC acting as both funder and technical authority, creating an immediate entry point for advisory support on regulatory design, training architecture, and capability transfer frameworks. KPMG's regulatory capability review, organisational design, and workforce strategy offerings sit directly in the path of all four mandates, and our existing relationships with APSC and AUSTRAC are the warmest doors in the portfolio. The pattern — multi-year capability commitments being locked in ahead of annual estimates — is precisely the moment when scoped advisory proposals land with the strongest mandate.

Risk & assurance

Regulatory enforcement pressure across risk and assurance is intensifying on three simultaneous fronts this fortnight. ASIC has codified a dual posture — 'easier to deal with, harder to avoid' — signalling that its 2026 strategic plan will direct supervisory resources toward entities that have not self-remediated, with home insurers named explicitly for cash-settlement shortchanging; KPMG's financial services risk and insurance practices have a direct opening with domestic general insurers who have not yet embedded claims governance frameworks. AUSTRAC is activating section 167 notices against Tranche 2 entities, moving AML/CTF exposure from legislative risk to live regulatory action for law firms, accountants and real estate principals — a client cohort PEPI reaches through government and professional-services relationships. TEQSA's 2026–30 Corporate Plan, paired with the AFR reporting of $2 million fines for governance and racism failures, converts higher education regulatory risk from theoretical to quantified; universities without board-level assurance frameworks are now priced. AMSA's Annual Regulatory Program 2026–27 and its published fatigue and falls safety data confirm a cycle of maritime inspection campaigns beginning now, with cargo-securing compliance a near-term enforcement target. Comcare's 2026–27 Corporate Plan signals continued investment in Commonwealth workplace safety oversight, keeping work health and safety assurance live for federal agency clients. Across all five regulators, the pattern is consistent: corporate plans are converting to named inspection programs and enforcement tools, compressing the window between signal and sanction.

State-gov priorities

Cited strategic priorities across all 9 jurisdictions, refreshed bi-annually. Every source URL is .gov.au.

Housing supply dominates the domestic agenda, with every jurisdiction except NT running a named dwelling-target program — from VIC's 800,000-home decade plan and QLD's million-home 2046 target to TAS's 10,000 affordable homes by 2032 — signalling sustained demand for planning reform advisory, social housing program assurance, and TOD feasibility work. A second convergent theme is industrial policy and sovereign manufacturing: the Commonwealth's Future Made in Australia, WA's Made in WA fund, NSW's state-owned energy and rollingstock push, SA's Hydrogen Jobs Plan, and QLD's 30-year resources plan all reflect a post-COVID supply-chain reset, creating KPMG opportunities in industry policy design, economic modelling, and investment facilitation. Energy transition is near-universal in stated intent but sharply divergent in pathway — SA and TAS are racing toward renewable export and green hydrogen while NT's 2025-26 budget explicitly prioritises mining, energy (including gas), and agriculture, and QLD's QRIDP is a 30-year living document anchored in coal and critical minerals, meaning a single national narrative on decarbonisation does not hold across state BD accounts. Health and social services reform is a cross-cutting pressure, with the Commonwealth's aged-care transition, NSW's safe-staffing mandate, TAS's 2040 healthcare plan, and VIC's decade-long Royal Commission implementation all pointing to workforce modelling, change management, and program monitoring demand. Law, order, and community safety diverge by jurisdiction in a telling way: NT's Crime Reduction Strategy and QLD's "adult crime, adult time" reforms reflect acute social pressures absent from the ACT, VIC, and SA priority sets, while VIC's Treaty process and CTH's gender equality strategy occupy political space that other jurisdictions have not yet entered. For BD purposes, the most scalable angles are: (1) housing delivery assurance across QLD, VIC, NSW, and ACT, where ambitious targets are running ahead of planning and construction capacity; (2) APS and state public service capability uplift linked to the Commonwealth APS Reform Agenda and cascading state equivalents; and (3) defence industry program support in WA and NT, where the Commonwealth's $330B Integrated Investment Program is creating regional economic strategies that require independent economic impact and procurement advisory work.

Last refreshed 2026-07-01. Bi-annual schedule; source URLs verified to .gov.au.

Commonwealth

  • Future Made in Australia
    The Treasury / Department of Industry, Science and Resources 2024-2034 (10-year, $22.7B package)
    Program design, sector assessment frameworks, investment mandate design, industry consultation, economic modelling, community benefit evaluation

  • Strengthening Medicare
    Department of Health, Disability and Ageing 2023-2027 (reform rolling); Budget 2025-26 expansion from Nov 2025

  • APS Reform Agenda
    Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet / Australian Public Service Commission 2022-ongoing (4 pillars, 59 initiatives; Public Service Amendment Act 2024 enacted)
